source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes), Eastern Shoshone chapter
place: Wind River (Shoshone) Reservation, Shoshone Agency / Fort Washakie, Wyoming
instrument: Fort Bridger Treaty of July 3, 1868 (exclusive-use guarantee) vs. Indian Bureau placement of Northern Arapaho, 1878
summary: The Indian Bureau settled the Northern Arapaho permanently at the Shoshone Agency in 1878. Shoshone attorney George Tunison argued this was done without Shoshone approval, and that from then on the government treated both tribes as equal beneficiaries, sharing Shoshone cession payments and allotments.
verbatim_quote: without Shoshone approval, the Indian Bureau had allowed the Arapaho to settle permanently at the Shoshone Agency in 1878
federal_account_contrast: Kappler/Royce treat Wind River as a single reservation created by the 1868 treaty; the federal record does not mark that half of it was effectively transferred to another nation in 1878 without a treaty or cession by the Shoshone.
map_implication: Annotate the 1868 Wind River reservation polygon: exclusive Shoshone guarantee breached 1878; one-half interest (1,171,770 acres) taken for Arapaho by administrative action, later paid for (1937-1939), not consented.
notes: CONTRADICTION inside the source: p.132 quotes Stamm that the Arapahos were moved in 1878 'only with the consent of the Shoshones', while p.135 (Tunison/Fowler) says without Shoshone approval, and the Supreme Court later ruled for the Shoshone. Both are quoted without reconciliation. Shoshone oral accounts reportedly describe a temporary invitation by Washakie, not permanent settlement; verify.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes), Eastern Shoshone chapter
place: Wind River Reservation, Wyoming
instrument: Agreement with the Shoshone and Arapahoe Tribes, April 21, 1896 (ratified Act of June 7, 1897)
summary: Per Hank Stamm, the 'most important feature' of the 1896 Hot Springs agreement was that the government made the Arapaho equal partners with the Shoshone in rights to the reservation, a change the Shoshone had not previously accepted. The Shoshone later were compensated in the 1930s for lands 'in essence, given to the Arapahos.'
verbatim_quote: the government made the Arapahos equal partners to the Shoshones in the rights to claim the reservation
sources_cited_by_source: Stamm, Land Cession of 1896 Commentary, Jackson Hole Historical Society (endnote 96); record of negotiations at National Archives
federal_account_contrast: The 1896 agreement appears in federal record as a routine joint cession; it actually functioned as a federal device to convert Arapaho presence into co-ownership.
map_implication: Tag the 1896 instrument as a joint-signatory cession in which the federal government treated Arapaho as co-owners of Shoshone treaty land.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes), Eastern Shoshone chapter
place: Big Horn Hot Springs (Thermopolis), northeast corner of Wind River Reservation, Wyoming
instrument: Agreement of April 21, 1896 (McLaughlin), ratified Act of June 7, 1897
summary: The tribes ceded about 100 square miles around the Big Horn Hot Springs for $60,000 ($10,000 per capita/cattle; $50,000 in five annual installments for 'civilization' and rations at the Secretary's discretion). Signed by Washakie, Sharp Nose and 271 others (273). Tribes conceded partly because the Big Horn Basin buffalo grounds had been destroyed by cattle and sheep ranches from 1879.
verbatim_quote: the sum of sixty thousand dollars, to be expended for the benefit of said Indians in the manner hereinafter described
sources_cited_by_source: Agreement text reproduced via Jackson Hole Historical Society; Stamm commentary (endnotes 95-96)
federal_account_contrast: Royce-style cession framing records price and area only; context (destruction of hunting grounds, money controlled by Secretary) is absent.
map_implication: Draw 1896 Thermopolis cession (approx. 10 x 10 miles at NE corner); note $60,000 for ~64,000 acres, mostly spent at federal discretion.
notes: Royce area number for 1896 cession not given in source; determine from Royce schedule (Wyoming).

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes), Eastern Shoshone chapter
place: Shoshone Agency, Wyoming
instrument: Agreement of April 21, 1896, signature certifications
summary: The interpreter certified that some signature names were duplicates but represented different individuals, and the acting agent (an Army captain) certified the 273 signers were a majority of adult males of both tribes combined. Majority was counted across both tribes, not per tribe. The source reproduces this without comment.
verbatim_quote: I certify that the foregoing names, though in some cases duplicates, in every instance represents different individuals.
federal_account_contrast: Federal record presents the agreement as valid majority consent; the combined-tribe majority and duplicate-name certification are signals worth scrutiny.
map_implication: Flag 1896 cession: consent measured as combined Shoshone+Arapaho majority; duplicate names certified.
notes: Interpretation (combined majority as a legitimacy issue) is this reader's, not the source's; the source only reproduces the text.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes), Eastern Shoshone chapter
place: One mile square around principal hot spring, Thermopolis, Wyoming
instrument: Act of June 7, 1897 ratifying 1896 agreement 'herein amended'
summary: Congress ratified the 1896 agreement as amended, granting one mile square around the main hot spring to the State of Wyoming and declaring the rest public land open only under homestead and town-site laws. The chunk gives no evidence the tribes consented to the amendment.
verbatim_quote: one mile square at and about the principal hot spring thereon contained, is hereby ceded, granted, relinquished, and conveyed unto the State of Wyoming
federal_account_contrast: Royce shows a cession to the US; the land actually passed in part directly to a state via a congressional amendment to a negotiated agreement.
map_implication: Mark the 1 sq mi Hot Springs State Park parcel as transferred to Wyoming by congressional amendment; boundary given in Act (start 1/4 mile E of main spring, 1/2 N, 1 W, 1 S, 1 E, 1/2 N).
notes: Whether tribes later consented to the amendment is not addressed; verify in National Archives negotiation record.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes), Eastern Shoshone chapter
place: Wind River Reservation north of Big Wind River (incl. Riverton), Wyoming
instrument: McLaughlin Agreement of April 21, 1904, ratified by Act of March 3, 1905
summary: McLaughlin sought cession of about 1.48 million acres north of the Wind River. After Arapaho leader Lone Bear left because his wife was ill, many Arapaho left with him; McLaughlin obtained signatures from 202 of 247 Shoshone men but only 80 of 237 Arapaho men, a majority of all men combined but a small minority of Arapaho.
verbatim_quote: 202 of 247 eligible Shoshone men but only 80 of 237 Arapaho men
federal_account_contrast: Federal record treats the 1905 cession as a consensual agreement; one of the two co-owning nations did not give majority consent.
map_implication: Flag the 1905 cession area: only 80 of 237 Arapaho men signed (34%); consent counted by pooled majority.
notes: Stat. cite 33 Stat. 1016 is reader knowledge, verify.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes), Eastern Shoshone chapter
place: Wind River Reservation, Wyoming
instrument: Act of March 3, 1905 ratifying 1904 McLaughlin Agreement
summary: After ratification, Lone Bear telegraphed Washington that the ratified version did not match what the tribe had signed. Separately, Mondell's legislation never promised to pay the tribes for the land; the US only acted as broker selling to settlers.
verbatim_quote: We think treaty ratified by Congress not agree with original treaty signed by tribe.
federal_account_contrast: Federal account frames 1905 as a cession on agreed terms; the Arapaho leadership protested immediately that Congress changed the terms.
map_implication: Mark 1905 Act as congressionally altered from the signed 1904 agreement per Arapaho protest; payment contingent on sales (no fixed price).

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes), Eastern Shoshone chapter
place: Riverton, Wyoming; 1905 ceded area
instrument: Act of March 3, 1905; Presidential Proclamation of June 2, 1906 opening lands
summary: Officials projected over $2.2 million in revenue; the tribes may have received only about $500,000. Near the end of 1906 elders protested they had received no per capita payments and no revenue from ceded land sold as Riverton town lots. By 1909 only 7.91% (113,743.68 of 1,438,633.66 acres) had sold; 8.97% by 1914.
verbatim_quote: tribal elders protested that they still had not received any per capita payments nor any revenue from the sale of part of the ceded lands that had been sold as town lots
federal_account_contrast: Federal record lists the 1905 'cession'; it was a trust sales arrangement that largely failed and underpaid the tribes.
map_implication: Attach payment-shortfall note to 1905 area: projected $2.2M vs. perhaps $500K received; Riverton town lot revenue not paid as of 1906.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes), Eastern Shoshone chapter
place: Riverton Project / Midvale Irrigation District, 1905 ceded area, Wyoming
instrument: Riverton Project (Reclamation Service), 1919 appropriation
summary: The Indian irrigation system promised from 1905 land sales was never completed. In 1919 the Reclamation Service took over and built the Riverton Project (now Midvale Irrigation District) for settlers, financed with money Mondell had allocated from Congress' appropriations meant for Indian reservations.
verbatim_quote: Construction was financed by money that Mondell managed to have allocated to it that year from Congress' annual appropriations meant for Indian reservations.
federal_account_contrast: Not in Royce/Kappler; diversion of Indian funds to non-Indian irrigation on the ceded area.
map_implication: Note on 1905 area: Midvale Irrigation District built with Indian appropriations for settler benefit.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes), Eastern Shoshone chapter
place: Riverton, Wyoming; land north of the Wind River
instrument: Wyoming v. EPA (10th Cir. 2017), cert. denied June 25, 2018 (Northern Arapaho Tribe v. Wyoming; Eastern Shoshone Tribe v. Wyoming)
summary: The Tenth Circuit held Congress intended the 1905 Act to diminish the reservation, excluding Riverton and land north of the Wind River; the Supreme Court denied cert in 2018. Interior's Solicitor and EPA had concluded the 1905 Act did not change the 1868 boundaries. Judge Lucero dissented that the lands were held in trust and about 75% of the opened lands remain in trust.
verbatim_quote: Today, approximately 75 % of the lands opened for settlement by the 1905 Act is held in trust by the United States for the benefit of the Tribes and their members.
sources_cited_by_source: 10th Cir. opinion and Lucero dissent (endnote 118); Tom Morton, K2Radio 2017
federal_account_contrast: Federal agencies (Interior Solicitor, EPA) and the dissent view the 1905 area as still reservation; the court majority does not. The map's boundary choice is a live legal and political question.
map_implication: Show 1905 area as 'contested diminishment': 1868 boundary per tribes/Interior/EPA vs. diminished boundary per 10th Cir.; ~75% still in trust.
notes: Source overstates the holding as land that 'belongs to the State of Wyoming'; the holding concerns reservation (Indian country) status, not ownership. Author opinion (p.139) calls the ruling 'a biased mistake'.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes), Eastern Shoshone chapter
place: Wind River Reservation ('district of country'), Wyoming
instrument: Fort Bridger Treaty of July 3, 1868
instrument_cite: RIT 373 (endnote 85); quoted via United States v. Shoshone Tribe, 304 U.S. 111, 113 (1938)
summary: In exchange for ceding a 44,672,000-acre territory recognized in 1863, the Shoshone received 3,054,182 acres 'definitely described' for their 'absolute and undisturbed use and occupation,' with no outsiders ever to settle there. This was then reduced by 1872/1874 (Lander/Brunot), 1878 (Arapaho half interest), 1896 and 1905.
verbatim_quote: no persons...shall ever be permitted to pass over, settle upon, or reside in
federal_account_contrast: Map should show 1868 reservation as guaranteed exclusive homeland, with later reductions overlaid as breaches/reductions rather than a static reservation.
map_implication: Draw 1868 Wind River reservation (3,054,182 acres) as promised exclusive land; layer reductions: 1872 Lander purchase, 1878 Arapaho half, 1896 Hot Springs, 1905 north of Wind River.
notes: The source (via the Court) calls the 1863 area a 'reservation' set apart; the 1863 Fort Bridger treaty is usually read as recognizing territory boundaries. 44,672,000 acres is the Court's figure.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes), Eastern Shoshone chapter
place: Wind River Reservation, Wyoming
instrument: Special jurisdictional act of 1927/1928 permitting Shoshone suit; Shoshone Tribe of Indians v. United States (1937)
summary: Congress in 1928 (per source) allowed the Shoshone to sue for violation of the 1868 treaty. The Supreme Court ruled for the Shoshone in 1937: placement of the Arapaho was a taking of a Shoshone property interest requiring compensation. The settlement required the Shoshone to recognize the Arapaho right to live on Wind River.
verbatim_quote: the Shoshones would be compensated for having shared their reservation for six decades
federal_account_contrast: The remedy was money, and it simultaneously confirmed the Arapaho presence; the Shoshone did not get exclusive land back.
map_implication: Attach to 1878 Arapaho placement: Shoshone won 299 U.S. 476 (1937); remedy money not land; Arapaho rights confirmed.
notes: Source says reservation renamed 'Wind River Agency' as part of settlement; name change timing needs verification. Jurisdictional act date commonly given as March 3, 1927; source says 1928.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes), Eastern Shoshone chapter
place: Wind River Reservation, Wyoming
instrument: Shoshone Tribe v. United States, Ct. Cl. No. H-219 (Dec. 2, 1935); United States v. Shoshone Tribe of Indians (1938)
summary: The Court of Claims valued the Shoshone one-half interest (1,171,770 of 2,343,540 acres) taken for the Arapaho on March 19, 1878 at $1,581,889.50, including timber and minerals. The Supreme Court (Butler, J.) affirmed in 1938 that the 1868 treaty gave the tribe the mineral and timber rights.
verbatim_quote: the minerals and standing timber were elements of the land itself
federal_account_contrast: Valuation used 1878 values for land taken in 1878; compensation substituted for land.
map_implication: Record the 1878 taking value ($1,581,889.50 for 1,171,770 acres, about $1.35/acre) as payment-for-taking, not consent.
notes: Per-acre figure computed by reader. Source's phrase 'mineral rights belonged to the tribe, not the federal government' is accurate to the holding.

place: Wind River Reservation, Wyoming
instrument: Act of July 27, 1939 (Shoshone judgment distribution)
summary: After attorney fees and interest, the Shoshone received about $4.2 million for 61 years of Arapaho presence; $1 million set aside to buy back land within the reservation; each member $2,450 ($100 cash, $1,350 credit for land, housing, livestock etc., $1,000 held in individual account).
verbatim_quote: the Shoshone Tribe would receive about $4.2 million in compensation for 61 years of Arapaho presence on Wind River
federal_account_contrast: Most of the award was controlled or restricted by the government rather than paid freely.
map_implication: Note on Wind River: 1939 award ~$4.2M, $1M earmarked for land buy-back (partial land return mechanism).
notes: Paragraph on p.136 repeats the Tunison sentences from p.135 verbatim (editing error in source).

instrument: Shoshone and Arapaho Tribes v. United States

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes), Eastern Shoshone chapter
place: Wind River and Big Horn River system, Wyoming
instrument: In re General Adjudication of All Rights to Use Water in the Big Horn River System (Big Horn I and Big Horn III)
instrument_cite: 753 P.2d 76 (Wyo. 1988), aff'd by an equally divided Court sub nom. Wyoming v. United States (1989); 835 P.2d 273 (Wyo. 1992)
summary: 1868 treaty reservation of land carried reserved (Winters) water rights. In Big Horn III the Wyoming Supreme Court ruled against the tribes' use of their reserved water for instream flow and let the state administer the tribal right. As of 2019 virtually no 'futures' water rights were in use.
verbatim_quote: This ruling allowed the State of Wyoming to infringe on and control the Eastern Shoshone's 1868 Treaty and legal rights.
sources_cited_by_source: Kinney 1993, Natural Resources Journal 33(3); Midvale Irrigation District 2019 report (endnotes 135-136)
federal_account_contrast: Treaty land maps omit reserved water; a paper senior right largely unusable in practice.
map_implication: Water layer: Wind River tribes hold 1868-priority reserved rights; mostly unused 'futures' rights; state administration per Big Horn III.
notes: Citation errors in source: Supreme Court cite printed as '49 U.S. 406 (1989)' (should be 492 U.S. 406); source labels 835 P.2d 273 as both Big Horn II and Big Horn III (Big Horn II is usually 803 P.2d 61 (Wyo. 1990)). Verify.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes), Eastern Shoshone chapter
place: Off-reservation unoccupied lands, Wyoming
instrument: Herrera v. Wyoming (2019) (Eastern Shoshone amicus); Wyoming House Bill 83 (2023)
summary: The Supreme Court held Crow treaty hunting rights survived Wyoming statehood; Wyoming dismissed Herrera's prosecution with prejudice in 2023. Wyoming's HB 83 then tried to define Eastern Shoshone off-reservation hunting on 'unoccupied lands' subject to state conservation; the Eastern Shoshone withdrew support, citing sovereignty, and the bill died.
verbatim_quote: treaty rights are not extinguished at statehood
sources_cited_by_source: Eastern Shoshone amicus brief; NARF; WyoFile 2023 (endnotes 119-122)
federal_account_contrast: Off-reservation treaty hunting rights are reserved rights on 'ceded' land, which a 'ceded' polygon hides.
map_implication: Ceded-land polygons for 1868 Fort Bridger should carry 'reserved off-reservation hunting right' attribute.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes), Eastern Shoshone chapter

place: Idaho (unoccupied US lands)
instrument: Northwestern Band of the Shoshone Nation v. Wooten (9th Cir. 2023), interpreting Fort Bridger Treaty of 1868

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes), Eastern Shoshone chapter

The author suggests both maps may be inaccurate and this could support Shoshone claims.

notes: Map not reproducible from text; obtain Robertson map. Single-source analysis.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes), Eastern Shoshone chapter
place: Vermillion Canyon, Browns Park (Brown's Pool/Park), Irish Canyon, Vermillion Falls, Moffat County, northwestern Colorado
instrument: Executive Order 13007 (May 24, 1996); Joint Secretarial Order 3403 (Nov. 15, 2021)
summary: Vermillion Canyon in Browns Park holds Fremont rock art and a medicine wheel interpreted as a Shoshone poha kahni (House of Power). Eastern Shoshone Sun Dance chief John Tarnesse identified paired figures as 'The Medicine Man and Medicine Woman.' Washakie reportedly visited often. The area is federal land facing unsanctioned visitation and petroglyph vandalism.
verbatim_quote: the presence of the medicine wheel in this Poha Kahni, House of Power, marks Vermillion Canyon as sacred land
sources_cited_by_source: Faris n.d. (Colorado Archaeological Society), citing Shimkin 1986, Stamm 1999, Hultkrantz 1967, Smith 1993; author phone call with Faris Dec. 8, 2023 (endnotes 137-152)
federal_account_contrast: Federal record treats this as ceded public land; Shoshone and scholarly sources identify it as a living sacred site.
map_implication: Add sacred-site point/area for Vermillion Canyon and Browns Park NWR (approx. 40.8N, 108.9W; verify), with return-to-trust recommendation.
notes: Source says the area is BLM-controlled 'as a National Wildlife Refuge'; Browns Park NWR is managed by US Fish and Wildlife Service, Vermillion Canyon is largely BLM. Coordinates are reader approximation.

summary: The author recommends Eastern Shoshone co-management with Interior, FWS and BLM under EO 13007 and SO 3403, and that Vermillion Canyon and Browns Park be placed in Eastern Shoshone trust; Colorado is asked to cooperate.

federal_account_contrast: Land-back proposal not present in federal record.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes), Eastern Shoshone chapter
place: Shoshone territory in (north)western Colorado
instrument: Indian Trade and Intercourse Act of June 30, 1834
summary: TREC recommends Congress compensate the Eastern Shoshone for illegal trespass 1834-1868, arguing the 1834 Act made the land Indian country, required trespassers to be fined and removed, and that resulting loss of game and land damage was never compensated.
verbatim_quote: This economic loss has never been included in any compensation for the violation of Shoshone rights.
sources_cited_by_source: 1834 Trade and Intercourse Act text (rec. endnote 1)

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes), Eastern Shoshone chapter

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes), Eastern Shoshone chapter

summary: Prime buffalo hunting grounds in the Big Horn Basin were destroyed by an influx of cattle and sheep ranches from 1879, so the tribes no longer hunted there; this loss was a reason they were willing to cede the hot springs in 1896.
